quote: so die aus der Physik etc stammenden Probleme die vom Verstande ausgeklügelten (Poincaré) warum?
english: so the problems stemming from physics etc. [surpass] those devised by the intellect (Poincaré). Why?
topic: Philosophical reflections on mathematical work: criticism versus systematising, Klein's applied versus Hilbert's ideal aims, why problems from physics seem richer and more intuitive (with an example from memory feats), layers of axioms, and the axiomatic method as the method of the future.

triage.modern_statement: This isn't a mathematical research question. It is a meta-mathematical, philosophical question: why do problems that come from physics and the outside world seem richer, more fruitful and more intuitive than problems made up purely by the intellect? Hilbert credits the observation to Poincaré. In modern terms it belongs to the philosophy and methodology of mathematics, close to questions about where mathematical problems come from and why mathematics is so effective in physics. No theorem or conjecture is involved.
triage.answered_by: Nobody has answered it, and it can't be answered as a mathematical question. Poincaré made the observation in 'The Value of Science' (1905), in the chapter on analysis and physics. Hilbert took up the same theme in his 1900 Paris address 'Mathematical Problems', where he discussed the sources of mathematical problems: the outside world and experience on one side, and the mind's own development of problems on the other. Neither text resolves the question, and it is still a matter of philosophical opinion.

evidence.claim: In 'The Value of Science' (chapter on analysis and physics), Poincaré argues that physics gives mathematics problems and keeps analysis from going around in circles. This is the view Hilbert's note credits to him.
'The Value of Science' is Poincaré's book on questions in the philosophy of science. It follows 'Science and Hypothesis' (1902).

In his 1900 Paris address, Hilbert explicitly discusses where mathematics gets its problems, contrasting problems that come from experience and the outside world with problems the mind produces itself.
The full text of Hilbert's Paris address, including the passage on where problems come from.

triage.why: The surrounding page is philosophical: criticism versus systematising, Klein's applied aims versus Hilbert's ideal ones, layers of axioms, and the axiomatic method. The note's 'warum?' asks why problems from physics are richer than invented ones, which is a reflection on how mathematics works, not a mathematical problem. It matches themes in Poincaré's 'The Value of Science' and in the preface to Hilbert's own 1900 address, but it is not one of the 23 problems or the 24th problem. The general topic, why mathematics fits the physical world and where fruitful problems come from, is still discussed in philosophy of mathematics. The sources I found don't show that this exact question has been studied as such, so 'active today' is marked unclear.
